title: JWT resource servers
summary: Let Spring Security validate incoming JWT access tokens and apply request permissions.

richText: A resource server protects an API using access tokens issued by a trusted authorization server.
It validates tokens. It does not create a password login endpoint or issue tokens.
Configure issuer-uri so Spring can discover the provider’s public signing keys.
JwtDecoder validates a JWT. Spring then creates authentication for the request and checks the request rules.
A scope names a granted permission.
By default, Spring maps token scopes to authorities with the SCOPE_ prefix.
Role checks use a different prefix. Configure a JWT authority converter if the provider stores application roles in a separate claim.

example.title: Protect journal reads with an access-token scope
description: Use Spring Boot 3.5 with the resource-server starter.
Set ISSUER_URI to the trusted provider’s issuer URL and API_AUDIENCE to this API’s expected audience.
Put the properties in application.properties. Put the bean in a @Configuration class.
Import Bean, Customizer, HttpSecurity, SecurityFilterChain, HttpMethod and SessionCreationPolicy.
The application already has a GET endpoint under /journal/.
explanation: issuer-uri identifies the trusted issuer and lets Spring discover its keys.
The Boot 3.5 audiences property checks that the token is intended for this API. Older Boot versions may require a custom audience validator.
A valid token without journal.read cannot read the journal endpoint.
HttpMethod.GET keeps the rule limited to reads. Other requests are denied.
STATELESS prevents Spring from persisting authentication in an HTTP session. It does not prevent database or cache access.
CSRF remains enabled. This GET request does not need a CSRF token.
The route permission still does not check ownership of each journal record.
